title: Over Here, Ender!
dateline: Terrinia. Years after the base fell.
mood: The Enders come back, and Chang’e stands alone in front of a shelter door. Across the water, one window is lit.

hero.alt: Lesley stands on a rooftop with her long rifle while white crescents wheel through the smoky sky above the burning towers.

segs.t: Chang’e was at the console when the base’s own alarm went, and the lab turned red.
Across the city the sirens had been going for some minutes. The last time the lab turned red, she had run out of its door between her parents. She did not look at the door now.
She lifted the crescents from their rack. They rose around her into a ring, white edged with pink, and began to turn. Mr. Bunny came to her shoulder.
In the corridor the researcher who had given her the big bench stood in her way. He had pulled a coat on over his nightshirt. Two others stood behind him.
“Where are you going?”
“Out,” said Chang’e.
“The Shield is coming.”
“The Shield couldn’t make my suits move.”
“Your mother would want you in the shelter.”
“She never reached it.”
He opened his mouth and shut it again. She went past him.
She crossed the red yard at a run, past the crater’s edge. The two guards at the gate were firing up the avenue at something in the smoke. They shouted after her. She did not stop.

Outside the gate the avenue ran down to the water. Fires burned along the seawall. At the avenue’s foot a pair of iron doors stood open in the seawall: a shelter. People were pushing through them, and a warden hauled at one door, ready to shut it.
At the top of the avenue, Enders came round the corner. Six, then more behind them, tall and gray in the firelight.
A man ran past Chang’e with a small girl on his hip. A woman ran beside them, holding the girl’s hand. The girl had her eyes shut.
Chang’e counted their steps without meaning to.
Thirty. Twenty.
At ten they were through the doors.
The warden saw her. “Get in! Now!”
“I’ll definitely protect everyone!” said Chang’e.
She took her place in front of the doors and turned to face the avenue. Behind her the doors banged shut, and she heard the bar drop.
The first Enders came down the avenue, and the crescents flew out to meet them.

She had built them to wait for an opening. A chest split apart to strike, and a crescent was already in it. The Ender fell, and the crescent snapped back into the ring and flew out again. Two fell, then four.
There were too many. They filled the avenue from wall to wall, and more came round the corner.
The ring spun faster. One crescent took a blow meant for her and cracked across. Its light went out, and it skidded away over the stones. Two Enders came through the gap at once.
Something struck the ring. The crescents scattered. Mr. Bunny went spinning away over the rooftops, and Chang’e was thrown back through the air.
As she fell, she saw them.
Two white coats, from behind, walking into a white light. Her own hand reaching after them. They did not turn around.
For years she had not let herself look at it. Now it came back whole.

media.alt: Chang'e falls with her gloved hand reaching out; then, in a white light, two figures in white coats walk away from her side by side while her hand reaches after them.

segs.t: She hit the stones hard.
An Ender stepped over the scattered crescents and bent over her. She pushed up on one arm. It gave.
Nobody to push me clear,
she thought.
Good. That was the point.
“Lesley, I guess this is the end of me. Where are you now?”
She said it to nobody. The gear’s log was running, as it did in every test, and it kept every word.
Across the water, high in the old tower, the window stood open to the cold. The moon hung over the bay. Behind Lesley the hard chair lay on its side, where she had kicked it getting up.
Down the stairs and round the water was minutes. Last time she had run, and been minutes late. From the window it was one round.
So she had stayed. She had watched the girl come out of the gate with her ring turning, and the iron doors shut with her outside them.

The tower stood up the curve of the bay, off to one side, so the avenue lay side-on to it. Every chest that opened toward the girl opened edge-on to the window. Lesley had held the rifle on that avenue from the first, and had not had one clear shot.
Then the ring broke. In the teal of her left eye the small figure struck the stones, and an Ender bent over her.
Ever since that day,
Lesley thought,
I vowed to keep you safe, Chang’e.

For years the base had been in her sights, every night. She knew the range to every step of that avenue. She knew how the wind came off the water after dark, and which way it pushed. It was still farther than any shot she had taken.
Under her breath she told the rifle Chang’e had built her, “Distance is just a number. There’s no target beyond my reach.”
On the far shore the Ender’s arm went up. Its chest plates parted to strike. The core burned inside them, but the opening faced the stones, and the girl on them.
Then I’ll stand in front,
she thought.
She turned the lamp behind her up full. Then she stood up in the lit window, where the Ender could see her instead, and braced the rifle on the frame.
“Over here, Ender!”
The Ender straightened toward the light. Its open chest came round with it, and Lesley fired.
The core went dark. The Ender crashed down on its back in the avenue.
Lesley stayed in the window, the rifle still on the frame. Now her hands shook, and she did not try to stop them.

media.alt: Lesley stands in a high window at night, the moon over the city behind the glass, her long rifle across her body and her face set.

segs.t: The Ender had straightened and turned toward the water, behind her, just before the crack came.
Chang’e turned around.
She looked straight up at one window. High across the curve of the bay, in the old tower, it stood open and lit, with the moon beside it. A figure stood in it with a long rifle.
The figure did not move. Neither did she.
She came,
thought Chang’e.
Her eyes stung, and she pushed her glasses up with the back of her glove. She did not wave. Then she got to her feet.
The crescents lay scattered over the stones. She called them, and they rose and found the ring again, one short.
The Enders up the avenue were still coming. Small craft lifted off the roofs and swung out over the water, toward the lit window. It flashed, and the figure was gone from it.
The window stayed empty.

The ring slowed. Every crescent dimmed at once, and the gap where the broken one belonged came round, and round. Her arm ached where she had landed on it. She did not know whether the window had been empty before the flash or after.
She held the doors anyway.
Then a round cracked from along the seawall, and the Ender nearest her fell. Boots came along the waterfront at a run.
Lesley stopped at her back, so close that Chang’e felt the coat against her shoulders. The rifle fired over her head.
The crescents flared. They flew out farther than they had ever gone in the yard, and came back brighter.
I didn’t change anything,
thought Chang’e.
Write it down later.
They pushed the Enders back up the avenue. Lesley went up onto the roofs and took every chest that opened below her. The crescents took the rest. Neither of them said a word to the other.
“Mr. Bunny, together!” called Chang’e.

Over the roofs, Mr. Bunny came back, at a size he had never had at the base: a great white rabbit-head machine, taller than the storefronts, his ears scraping the signs. His screen was as big as a door, and it showed his smile with the eyes shut. He dropped into the avenue, and the Enders broke against him.
That never worked in the yard,
thought Chang’e.
Not once.
On the roof across the avenue, Lesley looked up at him, then down at Chang’e. She did not ask.
Beyond the top of the avenue, a giant rose out of the smoke.

It was gold and black, taller than any tower on the waterfront, and its arms ended in long curved blades. It walked to the top of the avenue and stopped. Its head bent toward the doors in the seawall, and gold light began to gather behind its chest plates.
It’s the same one,
thought Chang’e.
Her legs stopped. They had stopped like this once, in the ash at the edge of a crater. She could not make them go.
On the roof across the avenue, Lesley turned her head. “Focus on the fight.”
It was the first thing Lesley had said to her since the crater, and it was an order. Chang’e’s legs moved.
She ran across the avenue and up the fire stair to Lesley’s roof, and climbed onto its rail.
“Console! Activate!” said Chang’e.
Panels of light opened in the air around her. Through them she read the giant’s chest. The plates were shut, and the light grew behind them. To fire, they had to open.

media.alt: A gold and black giant with long curved blades stands over the night city as light gathers in its chest and small figures rise toward it; then Chang'e sits on a rooftop rail behind glowing panels of light, reading them.

segs.t: It can’t fire shut,
she thought.
That light is the door in.
On her panel a red ring closed over the glow. Lesley knelt at the rail beside her, the rifle up. “Locked on!”
The giant’s chest plates parted. The light inside was gold.
Chang’e’s hand went out toward it. This time a crescent went with it.
Neither of them gave the word. Before the gold could turn white, Lesley’s round and the crescent went into it together.
The giant’s chest burst white from the inside.

media.alt: Chang'e on her pink crescents and Lesley with her rifle leap together at the gold and black giant over the night city.

segs.t: It rocked back from the water and fell the way it had come, across the top of the avenue, over the corner where the Enders had first appeared. Nobody was under it. Everyone from those streets was behind the iron doors.
Chang’e’s hand was still out. She closed it. Beside her, Lesley worked the bolt.
Before dawn two more of the big ones came over the roofs. They brought those down too.
Later the Academy would call the two of them the First Aspirants.
